learn.lesson1.p1: All pokémon are represented by at least one <bold>type</bold>. We could define a type as an "element" of nature; say, fire, for example. Types define the moves a pokemon is specialized in, along with their weaknesses in battle.
learn.lesson1.p2: This is done thanks to the power relationships between types, also known as <bold>type matchups</bold>. Think of them as in a "rock, paper, scissors" game. If your opponent chooses paper, what would you use to win? Certainly, you should pick scissors, because <italics>scissors cut paper.</italics> If you choose rock, however, you would lose the game, as <italics>paper beats rock</italics>.
learn.lesson1.p3: Now, let's recreate this example with a fire. If you want to put out the fire, What should you throw against the flames? You could throw water to it, because you know <italics>water extinguishes fire</italics>. On the other hand, if you throw grass blades to it, would it help? Not really, because <italics>fire burns grass</italics>. Thus, we could say <bold>water is supereffective against fire</bold>, and <bold>grass is not very effective against fire</bold>. So, to beat a fire type pokémon in battle, you should shower it with water type moves.
learn.lesson1.p4: This is the principle pokémon battles follow. However, with a current total of <bold>18 types</bold>, the relationships become a bit more complex. Here are the rules type relationships can follow:
learn.lesson1.p5: Sounds daunting, isn't it? Well, these rules become easier to learn when you find some logic to them. We could "cheat" by associating a phrase to a rule. Remember the phrases we used in the fire example? "Water is super effective against fire, because water extinguishes fire". We could create one of these phrases for each relationship: "Grass is not very effective against fire, because grass gets burnt if it enters contact with fire" or "fire is supereffective against ice, because fire melts ice".
learn.lesson1.p6: See? Just think about what would happen if two of these "elements" interacted in real life, and you'll have a closer idea on which move to choose to defeat a pokémon. (Okay... they're not 100% akin to reality and some of them might not make any sense, but you gotta pretend sometimes. These are fictional battles either way.)
learn.lesson1.nextLesson: Go to the <bold>next lesson</bold> to learn more!
learn.lesson1.attack: When attacking: (using a move against a pokémon)
learn.lesson1.attack.li1: A type can be <bold>super effective</bold> against another type, causing 2 times the damage the move would normally do (x2)
learn.lesson1.attack.li2: A type can be <bold>not very effective</bold> against another type, causing half the damage it would normally do (x0.5)
learn.lesson1.attack.li3: In certain cases, a type can have <bold>no effect</bold> against another type, causing no damage to the pokémon! (x0)
learn.lesson1.attack.li4: If neither of these conditions are met, the move would do normal damage to the pokemon. Also known as <bold>effective</bold> (x1)
learn.lesson1.defense: When defending: (a pokémon recieving the move of another)
learn.lesson1.defense.li1: A type can be <bold>weak</bold> against another type, recieving twice the damage the move would normally do (x2)
learn.lesson1.defense.li2: A type can <bold>resist</bold> another type, recieving half the damage the move would normally do (x0.5)
learn.lesson1.defense.li3: In certain cases, a move's type can have <bold>no effect</bold> against our pokémon's type, which means we won't recieve any damage (x0)
learn.lesson1.defense.li4: And in the same way, if neither of these conditions are met, the move would cause <bold>effective</bold> (normal) damage to our pokémon (x1)
learn.typeMatchups.info1: Click on each type to learn more about their strengths and weaknesses.
learn.typeMatchups.info2: Then, click on each row to show an explanation of the relationships.
learn.typeMatchups.p1: The most important matchups to learn are <bold>super effectiveness</bold>, <bold>weaknesses</bold> (and <bold>no effects/immunities</bold>, if they exist). You can prioritize learning those first.
learn.typeMatchups.p2: For now, resistances shouldn't be a priority to learn. However, they become important when you attack <bold>pokemon of two types</bold>. Learn more on the next page.
learn.typeMatchups.quizInfo: To reinforce your learning, go to the Quizzes page and select the <bold>Single Type Quiz</bold> option to check your knowledge! Can you guess the weaknesses of all 18 types?
learn.lesson2.p1: There are some pokémon who are represented by <bold>two types</bold>. All of the relationships we've seen so far are just for individual types. But what happens when you"re battling against a dual type pokémon? How do you know which attacks would be super effective against it?
learn.lesson2.p2: It's quite easy. Let's take a Charizard, as an example. First, Charizard is a Fire / Flying type pokemon. Let's start by writing all the weaknesses both types have.
learn.lesson2.p3: This gives us a close approximation of the types a Charizard would be weak to. However, let's take a look at these weaknesses. Flying is weak to ice, right? But we also know fire melts ice... what should we do in these cases?
learn.lesson2.p4: This is where resistances come into play! Let's list all the resistances fire and flying types have:
learn.lesson2.p5: To know which types a dual type pokémon is weak to, you have to list all the weaknesses both types have, then <bold>"delete"</bold> from the list any type that appears in the list of resistances.
learn.lesson2.p6: In this case, the <bold>ice</bold> type is one of the many types resisted by fire. Let's delete it from the list.
learn.lesson2.p7: So, if Charizard aren't weak to ice, what happens when you attack them with an ice type move anyway? Ice types now will cause <bold>effective</bold> damage to a Charizard. This is, normal damage, just like any other type not listed in the weaknesses and resistances list.
learn.lesson2.p8: Okay, so we have water, ground... wait, weren't flying types immune to ground type attacks?
learn.lesson2.p9: Let's move on to the possible immunities type combinations can have. Again, let's list all the immunities fire and flying types have:
learn.lesson2.p10: If any of the pokémon's types have at least one immunity, we have to delete it from the list.
learn.lesson2.p11: In this case, the flying type is immune to the <bold>ground</bold> type. Let's delete it from the list.
learn.lesson2.p12: There's an important difference we have to make here: immunities <bold>will still make no damage</bold> to our pokémon. So it doesn't matter if fire is weak to ground by itself; every pokémon with the flying type will be immune to ground type attacks, Charizard included.
learn.lesson2.p13: Okay... at this point you have to be wondering why rock appears twice on the list, right?
learn.lesson2.p14: There is an <bold>extra</bold> pair of type relationships when dealing with dual type pokémon:
learn.lesson2.p15: If both types of a pokémon are weak to the same type, then the type makes <bold>extremely effective</bold> damage to the pokemon.
learn.lesson2.p16: In Charizard's case, <bold>both</bold> fire and flying types are weak to rock:
learn.lesson2.p17: So, it's recommended that you prioritize rock type moves whenever you can, if you want to defeat a Charizard as soon as possible!
learn.lesson2.p18: On the same way, if both types of a pokémon resist the same type, then the type becomes <bold>mostly ineffective</bold> against the pokemon.
learn.lesson2.p19: If we take another look at flying and fire's resistances list, grass appears <bold>twice</bold>. Same with the bug type. So, don't even think about using a grass type move or a bug type move against a Charizard! It will barely make any damage.
learn.lesson2.p20: As you can see, learning the weaknesses of each pokémon can become tricky. We would recommend starting learning the weaknesses of your favorite dual type pokémon, or the most popular pokémon used by your rivals. And little by little, you"ll get an idea of how resistances work!
